details:
Mars in Moquegua: From Earth Observation to Mission Preparation

Mars in Moquegua is a browser-based 3D geospatial platform that helps researchers, universities, and robotics teams explore potential Mars analog sites in southern Peru. Our starting question is simple: could landscapes in our own territory support research and training relevant to planetary exploration?

The platform brings satellite observations and practical mission requirements into one interactive environment. Users can examine candidate locations, understand their environmental characteristics, and explore preliminary rover and crew mission scenarios.

How it works

The application uses preprocessed geospatial datasets organized into a one-kilometer analysis grid. It combines NASA datasets¿ including MODIS, EMIT, GPM IMERG, VIIRS, and SRTM with complementary sources such as TerraClimate, OpenStreetMap, and protected-area data.

These sources provide information about ground temperature, vegetation, rainfall, aridity, terrain slope, mineral indicators, road access, and environmental restrictions. Users can adjust requirements and inspect how those choices affect candidate locations.

The platform offers three modes:

- Test: Assess preliminary rover corridors against a selected slope limit, distance, and test objective. The system evaluates 16 candidate directions from a starting point, presents alternatives, and supports comparison with another zone.

- Train: Explore crew walking scenarios, select a potential habitat location, and estimate reachable objectives, travel distance, mission time, and return reserves using user-defined assumptions.

- Study: Examine environmental and mineral indicators, compare characteristics with reference locations, and review the sources and limitations behind the analysis.

Site information also includes the nearest support town from a predefined list, its straight-line distance, road proximity, and protected-area flags.

Benefits and intended impact

Our intended benefit is better preparation for field reconnaissance. Teams can compare locations and scenarios before committing travel, equipment, and personnel. The platform helps users move from “this landscape looks like Mars” to more specific questions: What characteristics make it relevant? Which experiment could it support? What constraints need further investigation?

We aim to connect universities, robotics groups, and researchers with opportunities for planetary analog research in Peru. Potential benefits include more focused reconnaissance, stronger educational experiences, and greater visibility for local landscapes as candidates for scientific investigation. These benefits remain to be evaluated through field use.

Tools and technologies

The application was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with CesiumJS for the interactive globe, terrain visualization, and geospatial scene. Google Earth Engine supported satellite-data processing and export, while JSON files store the prepared analysis data used by the browser application. Three dimensional models help visualize rover and crew scenarios.

The FOBOS assistant provides guided interaction with the application. Optional integrations with Groq or Google Gemini interpret natural-language requests into supported application actions; numerical results are calculated by the application rather than invented by the language model.

The core prototype runs through a local or hosted web server on a computer with a compatible browser and internet connectivity for external map and terrain services. No specialized field hardware was required to build the software prototype.

What makes the project creative

Our creative contribution is connecting environmental similarity with mission preparation in a local context. The same landscape can be examined from the perspective of a rover developer, a crew-training team, or a researcher. Combining candidate-site exploration, logistics, and preliminary mission scenarios makes satellite information more accessible and actionable for these different users.

Factors considered and limitations

We considered scientific relevance, terrain constraints, access, environmental protection, data availability, and usability in Spanish and English. We also considered the different spatial resolutions and observation periods of the source datasets.

The analysis uses preloaded data and does not represent continuous environmental monitoring. Displaying datasets on a one-kilometer grid does not give every source one-kilometer accuracy. Mineral detections are remote-sensing indicators, not laboratory confirmation.

Our simulations are preliminary planning tools. They do not detect individual rocks, loose sand, soil strength, or all real-world hazards, and they do not certify route safety. Terrestrial analog sites reproduce selected characteristics of Mars, not its complete environment.

Current status and next steps

We have a working prototype that supports site exploration, data inspection, preliminary mission assessment, and comparison. Our next step is to work with universities, robotics teams, and specialists to compare its results with field observations and refine the methodology.

Our vision is to help Peru’s landscapes become part of the research, testing, and preparation that bring us closer to Mars.
